**Finding: Compliant** (§ 9.4, paragraph p0039) — no redline proposed.

Section 9.4 hits the preferred position on all three material terms:

| Preferred requirement | § 9.4 |
|---|---|
| Customer convenience termination, 30 days' notice | ✅ 30 days, Agreement *or* any Order Form, in whole or in part |
| Pro-rata refund of prepaid fees | ✅ Vendor refunds prepaid Fees allocable to post-termination period; Customer owes only for conforming Services rendered |
| No Vendor convenience right in committed term | ✅ Expressly stated |

No early-termination fee or penalty appears anywhere. My document-wide sweep confirmed the Vendor's only exit routes are the mutual ones — material breach (§ 9.1) and insolvency (§ 9.2) — and § 24.4 additionally bars Vendor from terminating on our change of control. The clause benefits us, so it is left untouched.

**One item I noted in the rationale but deliberately did not flag here:** § 2.1 commits us to USD 2,000,000/year for three years on a take-or-pay basis "without reduction or termination rights." That language economically hollows out the § 9.4 convenience right — we could serve notice and stop receiving Services, yet still owe the full committed spend. It does not, however, remove the termination right, so it is a minimum-commitment defect rather than a termination-clause defect. Per the playbook's no-double-flagging principle (and the planner's steer), it should be addressed under the MINCOMMIT rule. Flag for whoever runs that rule: **the take-or-pay carve-out is the real exposure, and the favourable § 9.4 should not lull us into treating our exit as cost-free.** If MINCOMMIT is not in scope for this review, § 2.1 warrants a separate look.
